summary: Extends the Port Control Protocol (PCP) so that a mapping it creates can carry a human-readable description. It does this by defining a new DESCRIPTION option.

eli5.summary: When you ask for a door to be opened in a wall, you can stick a note on it saying what it is for. That way anyone looking at the door later knows why it exists.

questions: how to add a description to a pcp mapping
how to erase a pcp mapping description
subtitle: A PCP option that lets a client attach a short human-readable label to a port mapping.

tldr.problem: A Port Control Protocol mapping has no place to say what it is for, so an administrator looking at a mapping table cannot tell an FTP server from a camera.
tldr.mechanism: A new DESCRIPTION option (code 128) carries UTF-8 text in MAP or PEER requests. The server stores it, truncating if needed, and echoes the stored value back.
tldr.outcome: Support is optional on both sides. A server that ignores the option simply leaves it out of the response, and clients should avoid putting personal details in the text.

today: RFC 7220 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains an optional extension to RFC 6887.

sections.title: Why a Description Option
sections.content:
RFC 7220 extends the base Port Control Protocol (PCP, RFC 6887) so a client can associate a human-readable description with a mapping that PCP creates. It does so by defining a new DESCRIPTION option.

The option works in simple client and server setups and in more complex ones where an interworking function proxies between a UPnP IGD control point and a PCP server (RFC 6970). Querying a server to read back the description of an existing mapping is out of scope.
sections.eli5: It adds a label to a request so the door knows what it is for.

sections.title: The DESCRIPTION Option Format
sections.content:
The option has the option code 128, a Reserved field, a Length field and the description text. Its name is DESCRIPTION, its purpose is to associate a text description with a mapping, and it is valid for the MAP and PEER opcodes. The maximum length is 1016 octets. It may appear in a request, and in a response only if it appeared in the associated request. At most one may appear per message.

The Description field MUST carry UTF-8 text (RFC 3629). The text MUST NOT be null terminated, and a receiver MUST NOT rely on a NUL character to find the end, because the Length field gives the length. The Reserved field is initialized as in Section 7.3 of RFC 6887.

Example descriptions are "FTP server", "Camera" and "Network attached storage serve". How the text is used is deployment-specific. It might help an administrator when cleaning a mapping table, or in a portal-based deployment it could store a subscriber identifier.
sections.eli5: The label is just words, and a length number says where the words end, so nobody has to look for a special stop mark.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Support is optional for both PCP clients and servers. A client MAY include the option in a MAP or PEER request. A server MAY ignore it, for example if it does not support the option or is configured to ignore it. It signals that by leaving the option out of the response, so a client that gets no DESCRIPTION back knows it was not accepted. If the request had no DESCRIPTION, the server MUST NOT include one in the response.

A server SHOULD be able to store at least 128 bytes of description. It stores what it receives, truncating if it cannot hold the whole value, and MUST send the stored value back in the response. If the request contains an invalid DESCRIPTION, such as text that is not legal UTF-8, the server MUST ignore the request and MUST NOT return a DESCRIPTION option.
sections.eli5: If the clerk cannot write on the note, they just hand your request back without it. If your note is too long, they copy as much as fits and show you what they wrote.

sections.title: Updating and Erasing a Description
sections.content:
To change a description, the client sends a MAP or PEER renewal request carrying a DESCRIPTION option with the new text. The server runs the same validation it uses when refreshing an existing mapping. If the checks pass, it replaces the old text with the new text, truncating if needed, and returns the updated description in the response.

To erase a description, the client sends an empty DESCRIPTION option, that is, Length set to 0. The server confirms by returning the empty option in the response.
sections.eli5: To change the note, send a new one with your next renewal. To remove it, send a blank note.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
General PCP security considerations are in RFC 6887. In addition, administrators of PCP servers SHOULD configure a maximum description length that does not exhaust server storage.

If the client and server are not under the same administrative entity, the option can leak privacy-related information. Clients should not use it that way. For example, it should not include user identifiers, locations or names. The RFC points to Section 3.2 of RFC 6462 for a discussion of information leakage.
sections.eli5: Do not write secrets on the note, because other people may read it. The clerk should also limit how long a note can be.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA allocated the value 128 for DESCRIPTION in the "PCP Options" registry, from the optional-to-process range defined in Section 19.4 of RFC 6887.
sections.eli5: The number 128 was officially reserved for this label so nobody else uses it for something different.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Initialized as in Section 7.3 of RFC 6887.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the description text in octets, up to 1016; 0 erases the description.
